title: What a block costs
objectives: Count the parameters of a transformer block and of a one-block model, and check the count in code.

screens.title: Where the parameters sit
screens.prose: A block of width $d = 64$ has 4 attention heads and an MLP of width 256. Attention holds four matrices ($\mathbf W_Q$, $\mathbf W_K$, $\mathbf W_V$, $\mathbf W_O$); the MLP holds two. Guess before you count.

state.caption: One block, $d = 64$, MLP width 256: counts hidden until you answer.

screens.question: Which part holds more parameters?

options.text: The MLP, about twice as many
Attention, with four matrices to two
options.why: You counted matrices. Each MLP matrix is 64 by 256, four times an attention matrix.
Two matrices of 64 by 256 hold twice what four of 64 by 64 hold.

hints.text: Compare the sizes of the matrices, not how many there are.
Attention's are 64 by 64; the MLP's are 64 by 256 and 256 by 64.
Each MLP matrix is four times an attention matrix.

feedback.correct: Right: the MLP holds about twice as many.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Size each matrix before you compare.

byKey.attn: You counted matrices. Each MLP matrix is 64 by 256, four times the size of an attention matrix.
byKey.same: Two matrices of $64 \times 256$ hold twice what four of $64 \times 64$ hold.

explain.text: Attention: four matrices of $64^2 = 4{,}096$. MLP: two of $64 \times 256 = 16{,}384$, so twice as many. With biases, 16,640 against 33,088.

screens.title: Counting attention
screens.prose: Count every number in the attention part of the block, biases included. $\mathbf W_Q$, $\mathbf W_K$, $\mathbf W_V$ and $\mathbf W_O$ are each $d$ by $d$ with a bias of length $d$, whatever the number of heads, since the heads are slices of them.
screens.question: How many parameters does attention hold at $d = 64$?

hints.text: Each matrix holds $64^2$ numbers and each bias 64.
$4 \times 4{,}096$ in the matrices, $4 \times 64$ in the biases.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Four matrices of $d^2$ and four biases of $d$.

byKey.heads: You multiplied by the 4 heads. The heads share the matrices.
byKey.nobias: That leaves out the four biases of 64.
byKey.nowo: You left out $\mathbf W_O$ and its bias.

explain.text: Attention holds $4(d^2 + d)$: 16,640 at $d = 64$. The heads cut these matrices into slices, so their number does not appear.

screens.title: Counting the MLP
screens.prose: The MLP has $\mathbf W_1$ ($d$ by $4d$), $\mathbf b_1$ ($4d$), $\mathbf W_2$ ($4d$ by $d$) and $\mathbf b_2$ ($d$). Here $d = 64$ and its width is 256.
screens.question: How many parameters does the MLP hold?

hints.text: Count each array, then add.
$64 \times 256 = 16{,}384$ for each matrix.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Two matrices of $64 \times 256$ and two biases.

byKey.nob2: You left out $\mathbf b_2$, the 64 biases of the output layer.
byKey.d: You used a hidden width of 64. It is 256.

explain.text: $d \cdot 4d + 4d + 4d \cdot d + d = 33{,}088$ at $d = 64$: twice attention's matrices, since $8d^2$ against $4d^2$.

screens.title: The whole block
screens.prose: Each of the two layer norms has a gain and a shift of length $d$. Add attention (16,640), the MLP (33,088) and the layer norms.
screens.question: How many parameters does the block hold?

hints.text: Two layer norms, each $2d$.
$4 \times 64 = 256$ for the norms.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the three bars.

byKey.noln: You left out the layer norms' 256.
byKey.oneln: There are two layer norms, 128 each.

explain.text: A block of width 64 holds 49,984 numbers: two thirds in the MLP, a third in attention, half a per cent in the norms.

screens.title: More heads, more weights?
screens.prose: A colleague moves the same block from 4 heads to 8 and says the attention part now holds 8 times 16,640 parameters.
screens.question: How many parameters does attention hold with 8 heads?

hints.text: Do the matrices change size when the heads change?
Each head gets $64/8 = 8$ features: a thinner slice.
Still four 64 by 64 matrices with biases.

feedback.correct: Still 16,640: eight heads cut the same matrices into thinner slices.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the matrices, not the heads.

byKey.times: You multiplied by the number of heads. Heads share $\mathbf W_Q$, $\mathbf W_K$, $\mathbf W_V$ and $\mathbf W_O$.
byKey.double: Doubling the heads halves each head's width; the matrices stay 64 by 64.

explain.text: With $h$ heads each has width $d/h$; together they fill the same $d$ by $d$ matrices. The count is $4(d^2 + d) = 16{,}640$ for any $h$ that divides $d$.

screens.title: A one-block model
screens.prose: The timing spike's model: vocabulary 65, context 32, $d = 64$, one block of 49,984. Add token embeddings ($65 \times 64$), learned positions ($32 \times 64$), a final layer norm ($2d$) and an unembedding with bias ($64 \times 65 + 65$).
screens.question: How many parameters does the model hold?

hints.text: Add the five rows.
$64 \times 65 + 65 = 4{,}225$ for the unembedding.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add every row of the table.

byKey.tied: You left out the unembedding matrix. Here it is separate from the embeddings.
byKey.nopos: You left out the 2,048 position vectors.
byKey.nobias: You left out the unembedding's 65 biases.

explain.text: 60,545 in all: the block is 83% of it, and embeddings, positions and unembedding most of the rest.

screens.title: Counting in code
screens.prose: Write `block_params(d, d_mlp, bias)`, `model_params(vocab, ctx, d, d_mlp, n_blocks, tied)` and `count_arrays(params)`, which adds up the sizes of a model dict like `MODEL` (the reversal model of l14: vocabulary 11, context 12, $d = 32$, MLP 128, two blocks).
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

    ...

    ...

MODEL = read_model('sequence-reverse.json')
widget.how: Submit runs 8 hidden tests; each result must equal the expected whole number. Tests 5 and 6 count the supplied reversal model, `MODEL`, and check it against the formula.

mutants.symptom: Keeps the layer-norm shifts with bias=False.
Drops the unembedding bias when the matrix is tied.
Multiplies by the number of heads.

hints.text: Write the block first and reuse it.
Without biases, attention is $4d^2$, the MLP $2 d\,d_{\text{mlp}}$, the norms $2d$.
For `count_arrays`, recurse into dicts and lists and use `np.size` on arrays.

feedback.correct: The formula and the arrays agree: the reversal model holds 26,571 numbers.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check each part against the table.

explain.text: Counting the arrays checks the formula, and the formula checks the arrays: a mismatch means a missing bias or a stray matrix. For the reversal model both give 26,571.

screens.title: Without biases
screens.prose: Many recent models drop every bias vector, the layer-norm shifts included, and keep only the gains. Count the block again at $d = 64$, MLP width 256.
screens.question: How many parameters does the block hold without biases?

hints.text: Keep the matrices and the gains.
The two gains add $2d = 128$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Remove each bias vector and keep the rest.

byKey.keepln: You kept the layer-norm shifts; they are biases too.
byKey.noln: You dropped the gains as well. They are weights, not biases.

explain.text: Without biases the block holds 49,280. Dropping them saves 704 numbers, under 1.5%: the matrices hold almost everything.

screens.title: Tied embeddings
screens.prose: GPT-2 **ties** its embeddings: the unembedding reuses the token-embedding matrix (transposed), so it costs nothing new. Keep the unembedding's bias of 65. Start from the spike model's 60,545.
screens.question: How many parameters does the tied model hold?

hints.text: Which array disappears?
The 64 by 65 unembedding matrix is the embedding matrix again.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Remove one copy of the 65 by 64 matrix.

byKey.nobias: You removed the bias too. Only the matrix is shared.
byKey.both: You removed both copies. The embedding matrix is still there, used twice.

explain.text: Tied, the model holds 56,385. Tying saves one $V \times d$ matrix: 4,160 here, under 7% of the model.

screens.title: A large vocabulary
screens.prose: Edge case: keep one block of width 64 and context 32, but use a tokeniser with 50,257 tokens, untied. The table gives the parts.
screens.question: What share of the model is the embedding and the unembedding (with its bias)? Give a percentage to 1 decimal place.

hints.text: Add the embedding and unembedding rows, then divide by the total.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Add the two vocabulary-sized rows and divide by the total.

byKey.block: That is the block's share, the small part here.
byKey.emb: That is the token embeddings alone; the unembedding is as large again.

explain.text: When the vocabulary is much larger than the width, the two $V \times d$ matrices dominate: 99.2% of this model. A parameter count then says little about the block's capacity.

screens.title: Checking a model card
screens.prose: A vendor sells a news-sentiment model built on GPT-2 small: 12 blocks, $d = 768$, MLP 3,072, vocabulary 50,257, context 1,024, tied embeddings. Its card says 124,439,808 parameters. Your `model_params` gives 124,490,065.
screens.question: By how many parameters does your count exceed the card?

hints.text: Subtract the card from your count.
Then ask which array has exactly that many numbers.

feedback.correct: 50,257: one number per token, which is the unembedding bias. GPT-2's output layer has none.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the difference of the two counts.

byKey.tie: That is a whole $V \times d$ matrix. The gap is much smaller.

explain.text: The gap is 50,257 $= V$, so the card's model has no unembedding bias. A parameter count is the first number on a card; checking it tells you the conventions.

ideas: With biases, attention holds $4(d^2 + d)$ for any number of heads, the MLP $8d^2 + 5d$ at width $4d$, two layer norms $4d$: 49,984 at $d = 64$.
A model adds embeddings $Vd$, positions $Td$, a final norm $2d$ and an unembedding $dV + V$: 60,545 for the spike's one-block model.
Tying shares the $V \times d$ matrix; when $V$ is far above $d$ the embeddings dominate the count.

formula.name: One block
formula.note: Attention, MLP, two layer norms; heads do not appear.

summary.trap: Multiplying the attention count by the number of heads: the heads are slices of the same four matrices.

quiz.prose: A block has width $d = 32$ and 4 heads, with biases.
quiz.question: How many parameters does attention hold?

explain.text: Four $32 \times 32$ matrices and four biases of 32: $4 \times 1{,}056 = 4{,}224$.

quiz.question: How many parameters does it hold, with biases?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Two matrices and two biases.

quiz.prose: A block of width 96 has its heads changed from 6 to 12.
quiz.question: What happens to the attention parameter count?

options.why: More heads means thinner heads; the matrices stay $96 \times 96$.
Each head is half as wide, but there are twice as many: the total is unchanged.

feedback.correct: Right: the heads slice the same matrices.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Do the matrices change size?

explain.text: Attention holds $4(d^2 + d)$ for any number of heads that divides $d$.

quiz.prose: A model has a vocabulary of 2,000 and width 128.
quiz.question: How many parameters does tying the embeddings save?

feedback.generic: Not quite. One matrix is shared.

byKey.bias: The bias stays; only the matrix is shared.

explain.text: Tying removes the unembedding matrix, $V d = 256{,}000$; the bias stays.
